title: The City of Refuge
focus: Harlem as promised refuge and trap

teacherSummary.text: King Solomon Gillis flees North Carolina after shooting a white man and arrives in Harlem, amazed to see a Black policeman. He trusts Mouse Uggam, a fellow Southerner, who uses him to sell drugs. When the police come for him, Gillis fights, then sees the Black officer, and gives himself up with something exultant in his face.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The City of Refuge,” how does Fisher show Harlem as promised refuge and trap? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The City of Refuge, how does Fisher develop the idea of Harlem as promised refuge and trap? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The City of Refuge develops the idea of Harlem as promised refuge and trap. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The City of Refuge (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of Harlem as promised refuge and trap. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The City of Refuge suggests about Harlem as promised refuge and trap. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's setting and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Rudolph Fisher uses setting in The City of Refuge to complicate the reader's understanding of Harlem as promised refuge and trap. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The City of Refuge within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of Harlem as promised refuge and trap responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The City of Refuge alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of Harlem as promised refuge and trap follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The City of Refuge and its treatment of Harlem as promised refuge and trap. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's setting and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The City of Refuge as evidence for a larger claim about Harlem as promised refuge and trap in The City of Refuge. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The City of Refuge as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of Harlem as promised refuge and trap. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The City of Refuge.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the story for irony, dialect (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about Harlem as promised refuge and trap? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The City of Refuge develops the idea of Harlem as promised refuge and trap. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Fisher shows Harlem as both refuge and trap. When the text says “Harlem. Land of plenty. City of refuge-city of refuge” (The City of Refuge, paragraph 255), it shows this directly. Gillis dreams of "Harlem. Land of plenty. City of refuge," but his friend exploits him; yet even arrested he marvels "Cullud policemans," seeing the dignity he hoped for.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Racial slurs in dialogue; drugs; violence. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail. The text quotes racial slurs in period dialogue: decide in advance that no one reads them aloud, and name why the author records them.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes racial slurs in dialogue; drugs; violence.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
